notes.meaning: Joseph came before Pharaoh to tell him with deep respect that his father and brothers had arrived safely from Canaan. They brought all their flocks, herds, and belongings, and were waiting in the region of Goshen. Joseph would not settle them anywhere without the king's official approval.
Joseph chose five of his brothers to introduce directly to Pharaoh. He presented them so the king could see them and officially confirm their arrival.

Pharaoh asked the brothers what kind of work they did. They answered honestly that they and their ancestors had always been shepherds. They did not hide their humble trade, even though Egyptians looked down on shepherds.

The brothers explained that a terrible famine had dried up all the pastures in Canaan. They asked permission to stay in Goshen for a time to keep their animals alive. They made it clear that they intended to stay only as visitors, not to take over Egyptian land forever.

Pharaoh told Joseph that the whole country was open to his family. He gave them permission to live in Goshen, which was the finest pasture land in Egypt. Pharaoh also asked Joseph to put any skilled brothers in charge of the royal herds.

Joseph brought his elderly father Jacob to meet Pharaoh. Instead of asking for royal favors, Jacob greeted the king by praying for God to bless him. The aged patriarch spoke as a man of God with true spiritual authority.
Pharaoh was struck by Jacob's dignified appearance and asked him how old he was. People in Egypt generally lived shorter lives, so an elderly man of Jacob's age was a remarkable sight.

Jacob replied that his wandering journey on earth had lasted 130 years. He described his days as few and full of sorrow compared to the long lives of Abraham and Isaac. Jacob saw his earthly life as a temporary stay on the way to a heavenly home.
Jacob gave Pharaoh another blessing of peace and departed from the royal court. The king humbly received the prayer from God's elderly servant.
Joseph settled his father and brothers in the best part of the land, around Rameses in Goshen, just as Pharaoh commanded. He gave them homes and pastures so they could thrive during the famine.
Joseph supplied bread to his father, his brothers, and their whole households. He made sure every family received exactly what they needed, caring for even the youngest children like a loving father.
The famine grew worse and food ran out completely across both Egypt and Canaan. The people grew weak and exhausted from extreme hunger. They were wholly unable to feed themselves without help.

Joseph sold grain to the hungry people of Egypt and Canaan until he gathered all their money. Instead of keeping any wealth for himself, he faithfully brought every coin into Pharaoh's royal treasury.
When the people ran out of money, they came to Joseph crying out for food. They pleaded for help so they would not starve to death right before his eyes.
Joseph told the people to bring their livestock in exchange for grain since their money was gone. This spared them from starvation while keeping their farm animals alive under royal care.
The Egyptians brought their horses, donkeys, cattle, and sheep to Joseph in exchange for bread. Joseph supplied them with enough food to sustain them through that entire year.

By the start of the next year, the people returned to Joseph in desperate need once again. They admitted openly that their money and animals were gone, leaving them with only their bodies and their barren fields.

The people begged Joseph to buy both them and their land in exchange for bread. They also asked for seed so they could plant crops when the rains returned, preventing the soil from turning into wasteland.
Joseph bought all the farmland in Egypt on behalf of the king because the famine was so severe. Every farmer willingly sold his field to survive, and the entire land became the property of Pharaoh.
Joseph moved the people from the countryside into the cities where the stored grain was kept. This made it easy to distribute daily food and kept the people alive throughout the land.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many modern translations follow ancient Greek and Samaritan manuscripts reading that Joseph made the people slaves, since in Hebrew the words for towns and slaves look almost identical.

notes.meaning: Joseph did not buy the land belonging to the Egyptian priests. Pharaoh gave them a regular allowance of food, so they never had to sell their fields to survive.
Joseph gave seed to the people so they could plant their fields again. He reminded them that though they and their land now belonged to Pharaoh, they were free to cultivate the soil.

Joseph set a generous policy: the people had to give one-fifth of their harvest to Pharaoh, but they kept four-fifths for themselves. That gave them plenty of grain for next year's seed and for feeding their families.
The people gratefully thanked Joseph for rescuing them from certain starvation. They happily accepted their new status as Pharaoh's tenants, grateful for Joseph's kindness.
Joseph made this agreement a permanent Egyptian law, requiring one-fifth of every harvest to go to the crown. The only property exempt from this rule was the land owned by the priests.
While Egypt struggled under the famine, the family of Israel settled comfortably in Goshen. God blessed them with property, and their numbers multiplied quickly according to His promises to Abraham.
Jacob lived in Egypt for seventeen peaceful years under Joseph's care. His total life lasted 147 years before he reached the end of his earthly journey.

Knowing he was close to death, Jacob called Joseph and asked him for a solemn promise. He had Joseph place his hand under Jacob's thigh, which was an ancient custom for making a sacred oath, and swear not to bury him in Egypt.

Jacob insisted that when he died, his body must be carried out of Egypt and buried with Abraham and Isaac in Canaan. He did this in faith, knowing that Canaan was the Promised Land where God would one day bring his people. Joseph promised to do exactly as his father asked.
Jacob asked Joseph to take a solemn oath, and Joseph swore to do it. Relieved and thankful, the elderly patriarch bowed down in worship to God at the head of his bed.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Ancient Greek translations and the New Testament book of Hebrews say Jacob leaned on top of his staff rather than his bed, because in early Hebrew without vowels the words for bed and staff use the exact same consonants.
